author: William L. Shirer
biz: Shirer's diary is trusted because it was written on the day. Your weakest files at HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan will be the ones where the suitability reasoning and any vulnerability indicators were typed up later from memory. This week, require that the reason a product was recommended, and anything noticed about the customer's circumstances or understanding, is logged during the call or in the wrap immediately after, in the adviser's own words rather than a dropdown. Then measure two things against the previous month: the share of files carrying a contemporaneous suitability note, and the median minutes between call end and note completion.
Read your own paperwork as a hostile reader would

He convicted a regime out of its own filing. Do it to yourself. This week, pull every live advert, landing page, call script and WhatsApp template across both brands and read them as the Financial Conduct Authority would, marking anything that implies a guaranteed decision or rate, manufactures urgency, or would press somebody already in distress at Debt Support Direct. Fix or pull each one before the week ends. Measure the number of phrases removed, and then track complaint rate and the share of enquiries coming from copy you control rather than affiliate copy you do not.

b: William Lawrence Shirer was born in Chicago on the twenty third of February 1904, the eldest child of a federal prosecutor who was doing well and expected to do better. In 1913, when the boy was nine, his father died of peritonitis, and the family's position came apart inside a month.

His mother took the children back to her own people in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The household that had employed a maid in Chicago now counted coins on the kitchen table, and the boy went out to earn. He delivered papers, he worked summers, he kept accounts, and he put himself through Coe College in his own town, graduating in 1925.

What he wanted by then was simply out. He described the America of those years as fundamentalism, puritanism and puerility, and he had read enough to believe that everything worth seeing was somewhere else. So he worked his passage across the Atlantic on a cattle boat, intending to spend two months in Europe and then come home and find a proper job.

It is worth sitting with that childhood, because the enormous book he published thirty five years later is built out of its habits. A man who has watched a comfortable family lose everything in a month does not assume that institutions hold by themselves, and a man who has paid for his own education counts things rather than trusting impressions.

And a boy raised in a small town where almost everybody agreed about almost everything acquires an ear for the particular sound a crowd makes when it is agreeing. That ear turned out to be the most valuable instrument he ever owned.

b: The two months became fifteen years. He found work on the copy desk of the Paris edition of the Chicago Tribune, correcting other men's sentences in a city full of people who would later be famous for writing them.

On the twenty first of May 1927 he was at Le Bourget outside Paris when Charles Lindbergh came down out of the dark at the end of the first solo flight across the Atlantic, and he reported it. That night made him a correspondent rather than a copy editor.

From 1929 to 1932 he ran the Tribune's central European bureau from Vienna, which in those years meant covering a dozen small countries learning to be nervous. He travelled to India to report on Mohandas Gandhi, spent time in his company, and counted him for the rest of his life as one of the two or three people who had genuinely changed how he thought. In 1931 he married Theresa Stiberitz, an Austrian photographer, known to everyone as Tess.
Then, in 1932, a skiing accident in the Alps cost him the sight of his right eye. Weeks later, with the Depression closing newspaper bureaux everywhere, the Tribune cut its costs and he lost the job.

He was twenty eight, half blind and unemployed in a continent beginning to come apart. What he had instead of prospects was a trade, and the trade had one rule. Be in the room. Not near it, not briefed about it afterwards, but in it, with a notebook, writing down what was actually said.

b: In 1934 he was hired by the Berlin bureau of Universal Service, one of William Randolph Hearst's news agencies, and he reached Berlin in the last week of August.

He had missed, by weeks, the two events that decided everything. On the thirtieth of June 1934 Hitler had the leadership of his own private army, the brownshirts, shot without trial along with assorted political enemies, in the murders known as the Night of the Long Knives. The killings were a gift to the German officer corps, who had feared the brownshirts as rivals. On the second of August the old field marshal and president, Paul von Hindenburg, died, and that same day the entire army swore a new oath, not to the constitution or the nation but personally to Adolf Hitler. On the nineteenth of August a plebiscite approved Hitler taking both offices, with about nine voters in ten in favour.

So the army had sold itself, in six weeks, for the corpses of its competitors, and a popular vote had blessed the arrangement. That trade is the hinge on which the whole catastrophe turns. After the second of August 1934 the only institution in Germany with the physical power to remove Hitler had bound itself to his person by a promise its officers took seriously.

There was also something sitting in every German bookshop. Hitler had published the first volume of Mein Kampf in 1925, and it set out the programme without much disguise: living space to be taken in the east, France to be destroyed, the Jews to be removed from the life of the nation. Shirer's hardest charge against the statesmen of his day is not that they were deceived. It is that the plan was on sale, and almost nobody read it as though it meant what it said.

b: To understand the city he was now living in, Shirer had to work backwards through the year he had missed, and what he found there became the most disturbing argument in his book.

Hitler was not carried into power by a mob. On the thirtieth of January 1933 he was appointed chancellor by Hindenburg, lawfully, through the manoeuvring of conservative politicians who believed they could use him and contain him. On the twenty seventh of February the Reichstag building burned. The following day an emergency decree suspended the civil liberties of every German, and they were never restored. On the twenty third of March 1933 the parliament voted itself out of existence by passing the Enabling Act, which let the government make law without it, by four hundred and forty one votes to ninety four.

Then came the process the Nazis called Gleichschaltung, which means bringing everything into line. Through the spring and summer of 1933 the trade unions were absorbed, the other political parties dissolved themselves or were banned, the regional governments were taken over, and the civil service, the courts, the newspapers, the universities and the sporting clubs were all put under new management. By July there was one party, and it had been achieved with decrees, votes and signatures.

This is why the book frightened its first readers more than any account of mere savagery could. A dictatorship had been assembled inside a constitution, in about five months, by men keeping to the forms. Shirer's point is that the forms are not the protection. The protection is whether enough people with something to lose are prepared to make a scene early, while making a scene is still only embarrassing.

b: In August 1937 Universal Service folded. The International News Service took him on and let him go again within weeks. He was out of work for the second time in five years, with a wife, a baby daughter and no obvious future.

Then Edward Murrow, who was building a European staff for the Columbia Broadcasting System, invited him to dinner at the Hotel Adlon in Berlin and offered him a job in radio. The network's executives in New York were unimpressed by Shirer's flat Midwestern voice and wanted him to arrange talks by other people rather than speak himself. Murrow argued them down.

The argument was settled by Austria. On the eleventh of March 1938 German troops crossed the border and the country was annexed. Shirer was in Vienna and could not broadcast a word, because the Nazis now held the radio station. So he flew to London and, on the following day, told the story on air, uncensored, as a man who had stood in the street and watched it.

On Sunday the thirteenth of March 1938 Murrow and Shirer put together something nobody had attempted: a single programme assembling live reports from several European capitals, one after another. That broadcast is the ancestor of every news bulletin you have ever heard. It was invented because two men needed to get round a censor.

A month later, on the tenth of April, a plebiscite on the annexation returned over ninety nine per cent in favour. Shirer had watched the arrests and the fear behind that number, and he never again treated a reported majority as evidence of anything on its own.

b: The second great argument of the book is about bluffing, and Shirer assembled it from documents that only existed because the Germans were compulsive record keepers.

On the seventh of March 1936 German troops marched into the demilitarised Rhineland. They went in weak, and their orders were to withdraw if the French army moved against them. The French did not move. Hitler later called it the most nerve racking period of his life, and the lesson he drew was that his opponents would always prefer the next crisis to this one.

On the fifth of November 1937 he gathered his war minister, his foreign minister and the heads of the three services and told them his intentions. A colonel named Friedrich Hossbach took notes, and his memorandum survived to be read at Nuremberg. It is evidence that the men at the top of the German state were told in 1937 what was coming.

Then Munich. In September 1938 Britain and France handed Hitler the German speaking borderlands of Czechoslovakia to avoid a war, and Shirer covered every stage of it. What he learned afterwards, from the papers and the survivors, is the detail that haunts the book. A group of senior German officers and officials had been preparing to arrest Hitler if he ordered an attack on Czechoslovakia, and the agreement at Munich dissolved their plot by giving him what he wanted without a shot.
That pattern repeats until the bomb in the briefcase on the twentieth of July 1944. Men of conscience waited for the right moment, and the right moment was always the one just past.

b: On the twenty third of August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a pact of non aggression, with a secret protocol dividing Poland and the Baltic states between them. Nine days later the war began, and Shirer was in Berlin to broadcast it.

His working life now consisted of fighting a censor twice a day. Every script was read in advance by the propaganda ministry and the military, and he learned to say the forbidden thing by tone, by what he reported first, by quoting an official claim in a voice that invited doubt. Each night he opened with three words that became his signature, this is Berlin. In his flat he kept a diary he was not supposed to be keeping, and eventually got it out of the country in a trunk.

In June 1940 France collapsed. Hitler took the surrender in the forest clearing at Compiegne, in the very railway carriage where the Germans had signed the armistice of 1918, hauled out of a museum for the purpose. Shirer was there on the twenty first of June, close enough to watch Hitler's face.

What happened next is the best story in his life. Through a mixture of nerve and confusion about what had been cleared for transmission, he broadcast the news of the French surrender before the German government had announced it. For about six hours his report was the only account in the world.
By December he knew the Gestapo was assembling an espionage case against him. He left Germany that month, and he took the trunk.

b: Berlin Diary came out in 1941, edited from the notebooks he had smuggled home. It sold more than five hundred thousand copies in the United States, was translated into seven languages, and made him one of the most trusted voices in America. The point to notice is that it was contemporaneous. Not a memoir of what he thought he had felt, but what he wrote on the day, before he knew how any of it ended.

Then the fall. In 1947 the sponsor of his Sunday broadcast withdrew, and the network moved him out of the slot. Shirer believed he was being punished for his opinions, fought it in public, and left the Columbia Broadcasting System. Murrow was on the other side of the argument, and the friendship that had begun over dinner at the Adlon never recovered. It is a genuinely sad episode in which both men behaved badly.

In 1950 his name appeared in Red Channels, an anonymous pamphlet listing supposed Communist sympathisers in broadcasting. He had never been a party member. It did not matter. Radio work dried up, magazines stopped commissioning him, and for most of a decade the man who had reported the Third Reich to America lived off lecture fees and advances for novels nobody bought.
He was in his early fifties, humiliated, and in possession of two things nobody else had. Six years of notes taken inside the regime, and an empty diary for the next five years.

b: What rescued him was the paperwork of his enemies. The Germans had written everything down, and then lost the war too quickly to burn it.

In his foreword Shirer lists what was available. Four hundred and eighty five tons of records of the German Foreign Office, captured by the American First Army. Sixty thousand files of the German naval archives. Hundreds of thousands of documents assembled for the trials at Nuremberg, of which he obtained forty two published volumes of testimony and evidence, and a further fifteen volumes from the later trials. The diaries of the propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, of the Italian foreign minister Galeazzo Ciano, and the voluminous diary that General Franz Halder, chief of the army general staff, kept in shorthand.

That is the method, and it is the third great argument of the book. You do not need to speculate about what the men who ran Germany intended, because they dictated it to typists, initialled it, filed it and kept the carbon copies. The regime convicted itself out of its own in trays.

He was candid about the risks. Some may think, he wrote, that it is much too early to try to write a history of the Third Reich, and he conceded that no doubt his own prejudices crept through the pages. His answer was that the generation which waits a century for perspective loses something too, because it never knew the atmosphere of the times.

He worked at it for five years. On the seventeenth of October 1960 Simon and Schuster published The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich, one thousand two hundred and forty nine pages long. Expecting little from a vast book by an unemployable broadcaster, the publisher printed twelve thousand five hundred copies.

b: It sold more than a million in hardback, about two thirds through the Book of the Month Club, and more than a million again in paperback. It won the National Book Award for non fiction. For a great many ordinary families it was the first full account they had read of the camps and of what the documents proved.
The title carries his conclusion. A Reich promised for a thousand years lasted twelve years and four months, because a state built on one man's will and on conquest has no way of lasting.

Now the honest part. Academic historians went for the book, and much of what they said has stuck. Klaus Epstein set out four failings: a crude grasp of German history, serious gaps, no real understanding of how modern dictatorships work, and ignorance of current scholarship. Elizabeth Wiskemann thought it neither sufficiently scholarly nor sufficiently well written. German historians in the nineteen sixties condemned it almost unanimously, and Gavriel Rosenfeld, who studied its reception, records that it was even thought dangerous to relations between the two countries.

The deepest objection is to its spine. Shirer argued that German history ran in a straight line from Martin Luther to Hitler, and that what happened expressed a German national character which made obedience to rulers the highest virtue. Almost nobody accepts that now. Nazism is read instead as one case of something that has happened in many countries, and the regime as a scramble of rival fiefdoms rather than one blueprint unrolling. Historians comparing his manuscript with the published Berlin Diary also found a great many changes. Hugh Trevor Roper admired the book, and Richard Evans in 2004 called it a readable general history with good reasons for its success, written outside the scholarship of its time.

Shirer died in Boston on the twenty eighth of December 1993, aged eighty nine. What survives is not his theory of the German soul. It is the witness, the notebook kept on the day, and the discovery that a tyranny's own filing cabinets will hang it.

connects: Tooze's economic history of the same regime corrects Shirer where he is weakest, on what Germany could actually afford and produce.
Tuchman is the other great journalist historian of a European catastrophe, and both books are narratives of clever men sliding into something nobody chose.
Grove's rule about hunting for the Cassandra whose news you least want to hear is exactly what Europe failed to do with a programme that had been published in 1925.
note: Dates and figures here come from Shirer's own foreword to The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich, from Berlin Diary, and from standard accounts of his career and of the book's publication and reception. The source counts, including the four hundred and eighty five tons of Foreign Office records and the forty two Nuremberg volumes, are Shirer's own as given in that foreword. The Compiegne scoop is well attested, though the exact mechanism by which his report got out ahead of the German announcement is reported differently in different accounts, so it is described here in substance. The criticisms are given as the historians made them, and the Luther to Hitler thesis that holds the book together is now rejected by almost all specialists.
recall: What happened on the second of August 1934, and why does Shirer treat it as decisive?

President Hindenburg died, and that same day the entire German army swore an oath of loyalty not to the constitution but personally to Adolf Hitler. Five weeks earlier Hitler had killed the brownshirt leadership the officers feared. The one institution able to remove him had bound itself to him.
How was the Enabling Act passed, and what did it do?

On the twenty third of March 1933 the German parliament passed it by four hundred and forty one votes to ninety four, after the Reichstag fire of the twenty seventh of February and an emergency decree that suspended civil liberties. It let the government make law without parliament, which ended parliamentary government in Germany.
What was the first broadcast world news roundup, and why did it exist?

On the thirteenth of March 1938 Murrow and Shirer assembled live reports from several European capitals into one programme. It came about because the Nazis had seized the Vienna radio station after the annexation of Austria, so Shirer flew to London to broadcast uncensored, and the format was improvised to get round the censor.
What were Shirer's main sources, and why did they exist at all?

Captured German state papers, including four hundred and eighty five tons of Foreign Office records and sixty thousand naval files, plus forty two volumes of Nuremberg testimony, fifteen volumes from the later trials, and the diaries of Goebbels, Ciano and General Halder. The regime documented itself obsessively and then lost too fast to destroy the evidence.
What is the central criticism of the book?

Its spine, the claim that German history ran in a straight line from Martin Luther to Hitler and expressed a German national character of obedience. Klaus Epstein listed a crude grasp of German history, serious gaps, no understanding of modern dictatorships, and ignorance of current scholarship, and German historians of the nineteen sixties rejected the thesis almost unanimously.
recap: William Shirer was born in Chicago in 1904. His father died of peritonitis when he was nine, the family's comfort vanished in a month, and he grew up in Cedar Rapids delivering papers and putting himself through Coe College. In 1925 he worked his passage to Europe on a cattle boat, meaning to stay two months. He stayed fifteen years. He corrected copy for the Paris edition of the Chicago Tribune, reported Lindbergh's landing at Le Bourget in 1927, ran the Vienna bureau, went to India to report on Gandhi, married an Austrian photographer called Tess, lost the sight of his right eye in a skiing accident in 1932, and lost his job weeks later. In 1934 he reached Berlin, three weeks after the German army had sworn a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler on the day Hindenburg died, and five weeks after Hitler had murdered his own brownshirt leadership to make that oath attractive to the generals. Working backwards, Shirer found that the dictatorship had been assembled inside a constitution in about five months, with a lawful appointment in January 1933, the Reichstag fire in February, a decree suspending liberty, and an Enabling Act in March passed four hundred and forty one votes to ninety four. He watched the bluffs that nobody called, the Rhineland entered by troops under orders to retreat if challenged, and he learned later that Munich had dissolved a plot by German officers to arrest Hitler. He broadcast from Berlin under daily censorship, signing on with three words, this is Berlin, and he kept a forbidden diary. In June 1940 he stood in the clearing at Compiegne and got the French surrender on air six hours before the German government announced it. He left in December with the diary in a trunk. Berlin Diary sold half a million copies. Then a sponsor dropped him, he broke with the network and with Murrow, Red Channels blacklisted him in 1950, and for a decade he was unemployable. So he read his enemies' paperwork instead: four hundred and eighty five tons of Foreign Office records, sixty thousand naval files, fifty seven volumes of Nuremberg material, the diaries of Goebbels, Ciano and Halder. The book came out in 1960 at one thousand two hundred and forty nine pages, with a first printing of twelve thousand five hundred, and sold millions. Historians have since demolished its spine, the straight line from Luther to Hitler and the German national character. What they have never touched is the method. The regime wrote everything down, and a man with a notebook outlasted it.
stories: The flight that invented the news bulletin

March 1938, and German troops have just annexed Austria. Shirer is standing in Vienna with the biggest story in Europe and no way to tell it, because the Nazis have taken over the radio station. So he gets on an aeroplane to London and broadcasts it there, uncensored, the next day. On the thirteenth, he and Edward Murrow improvise something nobody has tried: one programme stitching together live reports from several European capitals in turn. Every news bulletin since descends from that broadcast. It was invented purely to get round a censor.
Six hours ahead of the German government

June 1940. Hitler takes the French surrender in a forest clearing at Compiegne, in the same railway carriage where Germany had signed the armistice of 1918, dragged out of a museum for the symbolism. Shirer is there on the twenty first, near enough to watch Hitler's face. Then, through a mixture of nerve and confusion over what had been cleared, he broadcasts the surrender before the German government has announced it. For roughly six hours, his report is the only account of the fall of France anywhere in the world.

In 1960 a blacklisted broadcaster who had not had steady work in a decade handed Simon and Schuster a manuscript of one thousand two hundred and forty nine pages about a dead regime. The publisher printed twelve thousand five hundred copies and braced for a loss. It sold over a million in hardback, two thirds through a book club, over a million more in paperback, and took the National Book Award. The paperback rights alone went for four hundred thousand dollars the following year.
take: Write it down on the day

Shirer's authority comes from a diary kept before he knew the ending. Keep a contemporaneous record of decisions and the reasons for them, because your memory will quietly edit itself to match whatever happened next.
Read what people publish about themselves

The programme was on sale in every bookshop from 1925 and almost nobody took it literally. When a rival, a regulator or a counterparty states their intentions in writing, treat the statement as the plan rather than as positioning.
Legal forms are not a safeguard

A dictatorship was assembled inside a constitution with votes and signatures. Procedure protects nothing by itself, so judge any system by whether somebody with standing will object early and in public.
Object while objecting is merely awkward
The German officers who meant to act kept waiting for a cleaner moment, and Munich took it away. The cost of speaking up rises faster than the problem does.
Someone is always probing to see if you will move

title: The Reporter Who Stayed in Berlin
